Can AI Companions Really Solve Loneliness?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1103 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • Sources indicate that engagement with artificial intelligence seems to be everywhere today, from education to medicine to business to making day-to-day life easier.
  • There may be incredible potential for AI to advance human happiness, health, and financial security.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

Sources indicate that engagement with artificial intelligence seems to be everywhere today, from education to medicine to business to making day-to-day life easier. Undoubtedly, some uses will prove beneficial, and others harmful. Evaluating the effect of different forms of AI engagement on human flourishing will thus be critical, and we believe our flourishing measure provides a helpful framework by which to do so. The effects of AI on flourishing may also differ across domains of flourishing.

There may be incredible potential for AI to advance human happiness, health, and financial security. It is not guaranteed to do so, and indeed, as per Pope Leo XIV’s recent encyclical Magnifica Humanitas (Magnificent Humanity), much of what AI does or does not achieve will depend upon whether the human person and human dignity are made central in the use and diffusion of AI. However, if employed well and equitably, the potential for AI to advance these aspects of human well-being may be substantial.

It has been revealed that the effects, however, of AI technologies on more humanistic aspects of well-being, such as meaning, character, or relationships, seem more ambiguous. Rich, developed countries already seem to be struggling with these more humanistic aspects of well-being, possibly in part due to technology. Will AI help or hinder our sense of meaning, our character, our relationships? As always, so much depends on how we use it.

In a recent development, AI technologies with various relational elements have effectively been used for purposes ranging from helping autistic children develop social skills to building the capacity of university students for civil discourse. While such uses arguably always ought to point back to real relationships, these systems may indeed have the potential to truly enhance human relationships.

However, there is another class of chatbots that aims not at enhancing human relationships, but at replacing them. These are chatbots whose principal aim and purpose is friendship and romance. In a recent article, we have argued that such friendship and romance chatbots have no place in a flourishing life. This may seem like an extreme position. After all, what harm is there in having loneliness somewhat relieved if one’s friends or family are proving disappointing?

The problem is that the temporary alleviation of loneliness is not a solution to loneliness. Loneliness, as painful as it can be, is experienced precisely to try to direct our attention, and our longings, towards deeper human connection. That can take a lot of work and time, and may not be fully within our grasp. But that thirst for human connection has a fundamental role in our life, in guiding us towards others.

Sources indicate that when AI chatbots have, as their goal, not helping us with human relationships, but replacing them, they will do damage—damage to ourselves, damage to those we might have interacted with, and damage to the social fabric of society. If they satisfy our loneliness, they do so without another person. A chatbot that always seems to understand, that never has needs of its own, that treats neglect with a delight to see us, ultimately makes us weaker in our capacity for real human relationships. We come to have unrealistic expectations of what to hope for in real human relationships. We lose the capacity to grow through the very difficulties and frictions that real human relationships entail. We come to focus on ourselves rather than on providing for the needs of others. Indeed, with AI friendship and romance, there is no one on the other side to whose life we have contributed.

It has been revealed that while AI may have some capacity to enhance our relationships (pointing us towards helpful books or resources for particular problems we are wrestling with) and while certain AI chatbot applications may benefit from relational elements (like the training programs above), this is very different from AI chatbots aimed at replacing real relationships. The effects of these are universally and comprehensively detrimental. They harm us, and they harm those around us. Even if we do not feel the negative effects now, or if they seem small, the increasing incapacity for social relationships will over time gradually erode human connection, human community, and the fabric of society. Human relationships are critical for our health and well-being.

In a remarkable turn of events, China, which has been very pro-AI, in July put into place comprehensive legislation restricting the development and marketing of AI tools “that provide emotional care, companionship, support, and other emotional services,” and including a strict ban on tools “excessively pandering to users, inducing emotional reliance or addiction, [or] harming users' relationships with real people.” What does China know that we don’t? They seem to have almost presciently anticipated the likely effects of AI romance and relationships on human society, human relationships, human reproduction, and human community.

There have also recently been some helpful legislative efforts here in the United States, especially for minors. However, we are naïve to think children are the only ones at risk.

According to recent reports, while we do think a ban on AI “relationship chatbots” for friendship and romance may be reasonable here (after all, we ban heroin in the United States), some might view such measures as too extreme. Even if so, we nevertheless believe every effort should be made in practice to purge AI friendship and romance from our lives as individuals and as communities. A technology designed to replace human connection is not a neutral technology.

Love—including love of neighbor and even love of enemy—is crucial for the flourishing of our society. In the words of Pope Leo (and others before him), if we are to seek a flourishing society (and to do so in the age of AI), we need to build “a civilization of love.” We need to love and care for one another. We need to be with one another. We need to have the capacity to work through the difficulties and frictions that real relationships entail, and to grow through those struggles. Therein lies our flourishing, for ourselves, for others, and for society. Real human love requires real human people.

#17694. This Is How Fast You Should Walk to Help Lower Your Risk of Death

📅 26 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1284 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Healthline ↗ Open Full Page

This Is How Fast You Should Walk to Help Lower Your Risk of Death

📅 26 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1284 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fresh research shows that how fast you walk, whether measured in a clinical test or through daily activity, can help predict your risk of dying from any cause.
  • The study compared two ways of measuring walking: a short walking speed test conducted in a clinic and the step rate people take in their everyday lives, measured with a wrist-worn device.
  • Both measures were linked to mortality risk and revealed similar ability to predict it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fresh research shows that how fast you walk, whether measured in a clinical test or through daily activity, can help predict your risk of dying from any cause.

The study compared two ways of measuring walking: a short walking speed test conducted in a clinic and the step rate people take in their everyday lives, measured with a wrist-worn device.

Both measures were linked to mortality risk and revealed similar ability to predict it.

The findings, published on October 23 in JAMA Network Open, could help doctors and researchers choose the best method for assessing health risks in different settings.

The study was part of the Whitehall II accelerometer substudy in the United Kingdom.

Industry observers note that it included 4,067 participants, mostly males, with an average age of about 69 years. About one-third of the subjects were female.

The researchers collected data from January 2012 to December 2013 and followed up through August 2024.

It has been revealed that to measure clinical walking speed, participants completed a standard walking test. They walked a marked 2.44-meter course at their usual pace. The test was repeated three times, and the average speed in meters per second was used for analysis. Participants who normally used a cane were allowed to use it during the test.

According to recent reports, for free-living walking measurements, participants wore a wrist-worn GENEActiv accelerometer for 9 consecutive days. This device recorded movement at a high frequency and used special software to detect walking episodes and count steps.

Recent findings suggest that from this data, two key measures of walking cadence were calculated: the median walking cadence (the middle value of steps per minute during walking periods) and the 95th-percentile walking cadence (a higher step rate indicating brisk walking). The study also calculated the average number of daily steps.

The researchers additionally gathered information on factors known to affect mortality, such as:.

National death records were used to identify deaths during the follow-up period.

Statistical methods were then used to estimate the risk of death associated with walking speed and cadence while accounting for other risk factors.

The models were adjusted step-by-step: starting with no adjustments, then adding sociodemographic factors, behavioral factors, and finally health-related factors.

The ability of walking measures to predict mortality was assessed using a statistical measure.

The study also examined differences between males and females.

The researchers additionally conducted analyses to test how well the results held up when they excluded early deaths, looked at subgroups by age and health status, and used different definitions of walking cadence.

During a median follow-up of nearly 12 years, 739 participants died.

Recent findings suggest that the average clinical walking speed of participants was 1.2 meters per second. The median walking cadence during daily life was about 75 steps per minute, and the 95th percentile walking cadence was about 112 steps per minute.

The study found only a weak correlation between clinical walking speed and free-living walking cadence, meaning the two measures do not strongly reflect the same walking behavior. However, both measures were independently associated with a lower risk of death.

After adjusting for age, sex, lifestyle, and health factors, for every standard increase in clinical walking speed, the risk of death was 23% lower.

Similarly, higher median and 95th-percentile walking cadences were associated with 17% and 18% lower risks of death, respectively.

When examining how well these walking measures predicted mortality, each on its own showed modest predictive ability.

Adding clinical walking speed to a model with other known risk factors slightly improved mortality prediction, while adding free-living walking cadence also improved prediction, albeit to a similar degree to that of clinical walking speed.

Combining clinical walking speed with free-living walking parameters provided a small boost in predictive ability, but the effect was not significant after accounting for detailed health factors.

The study also found that walking speed and cadence had similar predictive power for both men and women, although the overall prediction models performed slightly better for women.

Several sensitivity analyses supported the main findings. Results were consistent when excluding early deaths, focusing on healthier or older participants, and using different ways to define walking cadence.

Overall, this study suggests that clinical walking speed tests and free-living walking cadence measurements from wrist-worn devices are both useful in predicting all-cause mortality risk. They provide similar information but reflect different aspects of walking behavior.

The choice between methods may depend on the purpose of the assessment, available resources, and the context in which the measurement is taken.

Neha Sabharwal, PT, DPT, a physical therapist and director of rehabilitation specializing in geriatric mobility and functional decline at Vintage Faire Nursing and Rehabilitation Center in Modesto, CA, said that walking speed helps predict longevity because it’s an indicator of someone’s overall health.

“Walking is something most of us do without thinking about it, but it requires several body systems to work together,” she told Healthline. “Your heart and lungs have to keep up, your muscles need to produce enough force, and your brain has to coordinate each step while keeping you balanced.”.

Sabharwal, who wasn’t involved in the study, stated that in her work, she pays attention to when someone starts walking more slowly than before.

According to recent reports, “It is easy to dismiss that change as part of getting older, but there may be something else going on,” she stated. This could include muscle weakness, pain, reduced endurance, balance problems, or underlying medical conditions.

According to Sabharwal, the current study is valuable because it suggests that useful information about people’s movement can be obtained outside a clinical setting.

However, she cautioned against misinterpreting the findings to mean that simply walking faster will make you live longer.

“People who naturally walk faster may already have better underlying health,” noted Sabharwal.

“I would be less concerned about whether someone walks faster than their neighbor and more interested in whether they are walking slower than they did six months ago,” she remarked.

Theodore Strange, MD, chairman of medicine at Northwell Staten Island University Hospital and senior vice president of the Metro Market Region at Northwell Health, shared some insights for those who may notice their walking speed has declined. Strange wasn’t involved in the study.

“I mean, if it’s slowing down because a week or two ago, you were walking up a flight of steps with no problem, and now, you’re having some shortness of breath, I think it should be evaluated,” he told Healthline.

Strange added that if you’re experiencing aches or pains that weren’t there before, you should consult a healthcare professional, as they can make exercise more difficult.

It’s also essential to manage any chronic diseases that you have so that you can exercise as well as possible within the constraints of your condition, he mentioned.

It has been revealed that “And I think slow and steady wins the race here,” stated Strange. He suggests monitoring your walking with a device like a pedometer and progressively increasing your steps.

“Everybody talks about 10,000 steps a day. I think the most recent studies show probably 7,000 to 8,000 is adequate,” he said. You can start where you are and work your way up gradually.

Sources indicate that strange further noted that physical therapy can sometimes be helpful if you have concerns with gait mechanics, balance, or strength. Additionally, you might benefit from exercise that is tailored to your condition, for example, if you’ve had a stroke.

Finally, Strange advised stretching before and after exercise to keep your muscles moving.

“I go back to adequate nutrition and hydration being vital,” he said. You want to make sure you are adequately supporting your body’s ability to exercise, said Strange.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the Rogue is by far Nissan’s best seller in the United States, with the brand shifting more than 200,000 units of the compact crossover last year. So the tech giant can’t afford to screw with it whimsically. That’s why there are soon to be two Rogues. The regular version will continue to be produced by Nissan’s giant plant in Smyrna, Tennessee. And the newly introduced 2027 Rogue Hybrid tested here will be imported from Japan. Despite its name, the Hybrid isn’t just to keep up with gasoline-electric rivals—it’s a fundamental step beyond them.

It has been revealed that our expert editors test every vehicle we review. Read more about how we test and review cars here.

Nissan has offered hybrid versions of the Rogue, off and on, since the 2017 model year, including a 2026 plug-in hybrid, which was a thinly disguised Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV (itself based on the Rogue). This Rogue Hybrid, though, is a newly introduced twist for Nissan. It’s not a parallel hybrid like the archrival Toyota RAV4 but a serial hybrid, similar to the sometimes fondly misremembered Chevrolet Volt.

Industry observers note that A serial hybrid is, to oversimplify only slightly, an electric powertrain lashed to an internal-combustion engine that acts as a generator to produce current. That current is delivered to a battery and electric motors that do the propulsive work. There is no direct, mechanical drive from engine to road; traction is all delivered electrically. Like a diesel-electric railroad locomotive. That spares buyers the need to live with a constantly variable transmission. For which, hallelujah.

The engine is a 1.5-liter turbocharged three-cylinder making 148 hp and 171 lb-ft in its own right and working in conjunction with a dinky 1.67-kWh lithium-ion battery pack. Drive is delivered through two electric motors, one turning each axle, with a peak system output quoted at 225 hp.

Recent findings suggest that since this is an electric crossover that happens to have an internal-combustion engine aboard, it drives very much like other electrics. That includes one-pedal driving with regenerative braking in “e-Pedal” mode. It’s more Leaf than Pathfinder or regular Rogue.

It has been revealed that historically, Nissan has done a great job of tuning every Rogue’s suspension for its duty of prowling across every obstacle suburbia throws at it. It crosses Costco speed bumps confidently, doesn’t chunk up when sliding across a curb during parallel parking, and steers precisely and confidently when sneaking into a garage full of bicycles and long disused exercise equipment.

Industry observers note that the dry roads of Santa Barbara County in October are no challenge for any all-wheel-drive system. That in mind, the Rogue Hybrid makes effective use of its 235-mm-wide all-season radials (on 18-inch wheels in the base SV and 19s with the SR and Platinum). With much of its battery and electric motor weight carried low, Nissan claims a weight distribution of 56 percent front and 44 percent rear for the test vehicle. The conventional Rogue carries about 60 percent of its weight on its nose.

According to recent reports, and then there’s the engine itself. The inline-three runs on the Miller cycle and has a relatively large turbocharger that spools up to keep the engine at its torque peak easily. The engine won’t spin past 5200 rpm, and since all it does is send juice to the motor and battery pack, there was no way for me to push it past that low redline.

According to recent reports, this is not a fire-breathing electric. Acceleration is nicely linear as with, say, the Leaf or a Chevrolet Bolt. Because 225 hp can push two tons and then some only so promptly, 0–60 is likely in the mid-six-second range, and the quarter-mile will be just under 16-seconds. It’s roughly comparable to the Leaf.

As nonplussed as the acceleration times will leave those who love to drive, there is the compensation of outstanding fuel economy. The EPA rates the latest Rogue Hybrid SR at 41 mpg in the city, 36 mpg on the highway, and 38 mpg combined. That’s up a huge 12 mpg in the city cycle compared with the conventional Rogue Platinum AWD, along with a smaller 4 mpg on the highway and a modest 9 mpg combined.

Recent findings suggest that the rest of the Rogue Hybrid’s mechanical substance is familiar stuff. Many of the structural elements and suspension design carryover from the current conventional Rogue, along with the 106.5-inch wheelbase. The Rogue Hybrid’s 72.8-inch overall width is up 0.4 inch, and the 67.2-inch overall height is down 0.2 inch. Nissan isn’t screwing with what’s working.

Nissan’s interior designers have done an outstanding job of making the fresh Rogue Hybrid feel roomy. The dash is relatively low below the windshield, and the door panels are shaped for some elbowroom. The seats are also well considered and cushy, which in this class of vehicle is what matters. Eight-way power-adjustable and heated front seats are standard across the line, with the Platinum trim also getting ventilation for cooling and a memory feature. Like giant moonroofs? One comes standard on the Platinum and optional on the lesser trims.

According to recent reports, then there are the Platinum’s massive twin 14.3-inch screens across a common plane. It’s pretty much the same setup as used in the better Leaf models. And the graphics are similar as well. The best feature is the Platinum’s head-up display, which is all kinds of wicked cool.

Also aboard is Nissan’s ProPilot Assist semi-autonomous system, which allows hands-free driving for extended periods. On known, well-marked roads, I found that it worked well.

In a recent development, however, carrying around two powertrains induces pudginess. Nissan lists the conventional 2027 Rogue at between 3444 and 3534 pounds, depending on trim level. The Rogue Hybrid comes in between 4065 and 4167 pounds.

Nissan lists the gross vehicle weight rating of the pure combustion Rogue at 4641 pounds and the Hybrid’s at 5192 pounds. That means that the Hybrid is down in lugging by about 100 pounds—two large suitcases or one large dog. So, pack light and adopt smaller dogs.

The Rogue competes in the toughest part of the current automotive market: compact crossovers. Virtually every manufacturer’s best seller is in this class, with an increasing percentage of the vehicles being hybrid.

Priced across the line to compete with Toyota’s all-hybrid RAV4 line, the Rogue Hybrid is a solid alternative, although the RAV4 AWD is more efficient on every EPA figure. But as Toyota dealers are often constrained by supply issues, so there could be more price flexibility at the Nissan stores.

According to recent reports, the other obvious rival is the Honda CR-V Hybrid, which uses a similar but subtly different powertrain from the Rogue Hybrid, this combining a primary electric drive motor with a lockup clutch that can mechanically link the engine to the wheels at higher speeds. The Rogue has a slight advantage on EPA mpg figures when compared with the all-wheel-drive version of the Honda, but the front-wheel-drive CR-V Hybrid is less expensive and better on gas.

Industry observers note that the Rogue Hybrid’s nose has an odd funkiness about it. In the SR (with Tech package) that was on hand, most of the upper grille is blocked off. The indentations are more the suggestion of cooling than actual cooling. And the relatively small multipart headlights are surrounded by decorative lighting mostly to balance out the large simulated grille.

What Is the Strongest Predictor of Divorce?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (754 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.
  • It has been revealed that how do you avoid getting divorced?
  • Getting divorced increases one’s risk of experiencing financial strain, drug and alcohol abuse, suicide, poorer health, and interrupted parenting if the couple has children.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.

It has been revealed that how do you avoid getting divorced? By definition, all married couples seek to avoid their marriage falling apart. In wedding ceremonial vows, couples make commitments to each other, which typically include standing by one another’s side in sickness and health, and in times of prosperity and poverty. Marriage is meant to last forever, but it doesn’t always work out as intended. In the United States, 43-46 percent of marriages end in divorce, and that number rises for second or third marriages.1.

Divorce is painful and costly. Getting divorced increases one’s risk of experiencing financial strain, drug and alcohol abuse, suicide, poorer health, and interrupted parenting if the couple has children. Despite the high prevalence of divorce and the substantial consequences associated with it, research on why marriages end has largely developed in separate camps: one focused on how couples communicate, another on the personal vulnerabilities each spouse brings into the marriage, and a third on couples’ financial and socioeconomic circumstances. These perspectives had never been directly compared to see which best predicts divorce. Recently, a team of social scientists published an article digging deep into this question.2.

In a recent development, the researchers began by recruiting 368 heterosexual newlywed couples from the Los Angeles Project on Newlywed Development who had gotten married within the past 6 months. The study began in 2009-10 and concluded in 2021-22. Over these 12 years, the researchers tracked a variety of metrics from the couples and, of primary interest, which couples got divorced (or were separated). Six key predictor variables were collected, which include:.

It has been revealed that the vulnerability variables included a score composed of adverse childhood experiences, history of physical/sexual abuse, problematic substance use (past 9 months), negative affect (past 30 days), and parents’ marital status. Communication style was assessed by video recording couples’ discussion of a topic or problem in their relationship, which was carefully coded by trained research assistants. Socioeconomic status included typical metrics of education, income, work stability, financial strain, and neighborhood median income. Worth noting is that the sample itself was not necessarily representative of the general U.S. population (lower income than average, largely Hispanic).

By the end of the study, 39 percent of couples were divorced. When all six of the key predictor variables listed above were used together to estimate who got divorced, the evidence pointed to the wife’s vulnerabilities as the only statistically significant predictor of divorce. The wife’s vulnerabilities also predicted a secondary variable measuring how swiftly couples ended their marriage. In other words, the more of these vulnerabilities a wife reported (adverse childhood experiences, physical/sexual abuse, problematic substance use, frequent negative emotions in the top 25 percent of the sample, or not being raised by married parents), the more likely the couple was to divorce, even after accounting for the other five predictors.

Although speculative, the authors propose a few reasons why this finding occurred. Women tend to handle the lion’s share of domestic and emotional labor in marriages. Women also tend to be more responsive to partners’ needs, have better memory and awareness of relationship events, and notice problems more often. In sum, women with more vulnerabilities may be more likely to reach the decision to exit more often and more swiftly.

Industry observers note that but are vulnerabilities deterministic of divorce? Not quite. The same study found that communication mattered in an notable way. Among couples who communicated especially well, including more warmth, humor, and effective problem solving, and less hostility, the added divorce risk tied to wives’ vulnerabilities largely disappeared. The baggage women carry into a marriage appears real, but strong interpersonal communication seems to buffer against it. The findings point to two places worth investing in: reducing childhood adversity in the first place and offering couples support that works with those personal histories. Knowing where the risk lies doesn’t seal a couple’s fate. It tells them where to put in the work.

Recent findings suggest that 1. Amato, P. R. (2010). Research on divorce: Continuing trends and upcoming developments. Journal of Marriage and Family, 72(3), 650–666.

It has been revealed that 2. Smith, M. G., Block, J. M., Bradbury, T. N., & Karney, B. R. (2026). Individual, interpersonal, and socioeconomic predictors of divorce: A 12-year prospective study. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. Advance online publication. https://dx.doi.org/10.1037/pspi0000537.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“A house is really a life…one you’ve had or one you want to have. A upcoming dream.” So wrote Shirley MacLaine on the first page of her memoir Sage-ing While Age-ing. And she should know. The dancer-actor-author has lived everywhere from the family home at 930 North Liberty Street in Richmond, Virginia, which she shared with her parents and younger brother (none other than Warren Beatty) to Manhattan apartments, Malibu beach cottages, and New Mexican desert ranches. And that’s just in this lifetime; MacLaine believes she has come around again through several incarnations, even writing books about her experience as a nongendered being in the Lemurian era, and another go-round on the lost continent of Atlantis.

In the 10 images below, we focus on MacLaine’s current incarnation, stepping into the Oscar-winner’s homes to see the star of Steel Magnolias and Downton Abbey at work, at play, and dancing on air.

MacLaine relaxes with a magazine in 1954.

It has been revealed that at 20, MacLaine was a chorus girl on Broadway and the understudy for Carol Haney in The Pajama Game. When Haney twisted her ankle, MacLaine (who had changed her last name from Beaty to an alternate spelling of her mother’s maiden name, MacLean), replaced her for two weeks. Alfred Hitchcock spotted her and cast her in The Trouble with Harry, and Hal Walis signed her to a five-year studio contract, which led her to move to California. This 1954 shot highlights her reading a magazine at home in Malibu, where she rented a tiny beachfront apartment. “Each home was a palace and a new jolt. They loomed on cultivated hilltops or nestled in L-shapes and U-shapes on shaded slopes, jewel-like habitations set in acres of jade carpet,” MacLaine recalled in her memoir Don’t Fall Off the Mountain. “We stared at the fairyland until our eyes hurt and our sense of reality reminded us that we were flat broke.”.

When MacLaine moved from Fresh York to California, she writes in Don’t Fall Off the Mountain, “sunshine bled from every corner and the dazzling white buildings gave me a permanent squint.” The happy gaze is on full display here in on the beach in front of the Malibu one-bedroom she and husband Steve Parker rented, which was not white, but a weathered wood cottage on stilts.

MacLaine and Parker, making the most of their outdoor shower in 1955.

According to recent reports, “When I met Steve Parker, the attraction was immediate,” MacLaine writes in her photo-driven memoir The Wall of Life. She first encountered the businessman in Newly introduced York, where, before he proposed, he informed her he was “undercover with military intelligence and work in Japan regularly, as well as other places throughout the world.” Here, Parker sneaks up on MacLaine in the one-bedroom, one-bathroom Malibu pad’s bonus outdoor shower.

The newlyweds on their home’s deck in Malibu in March, 1955.

This 1955 shot captures a rare moment of togetherness for MacLaine and Parker at their Malibu beach house. He often lived in Japan while she made films. “I’m not sure I would say that Steve and I had a happy marriage, but it was a satisfied one,” MacLaine wrote in The Wall of Life. “He had a mistress in Japan and I had whoever I was with.” But in their SoCal haven, they experienced their first taste of married life. “I was up every morning at four-thirty trying to be a housewife—ironing cleaning, and experimenting with the cookbook,” MacLaine wrote in Don’t Fall Off the Mountain. “At six Steve drove me to the studio, where we shot the final sequences of The Trouble with Harry.”.

MacLaine dancing on the beach in front of her home in Malibu.

Sources indicate that macLaine, shown here leaping on the beach in front of her home, trained as a dancer since age three. “As I recall my life, I have come to understand that the physicality of dance was the most influential force,” she wrote in The Wall of Life. Here, MacLaine highlights of her skills at the rental property she described in Don’t Fall Off the Mountain as “a tiny, one-bedroom apartment in a building set high on pilings that shook with each wave that crashed beneath it.”.

Parker helps MacLaine study a script.

This 1955 publicity shot indicates MacLaine studying a script under Parker’s adoring eye in their Malibu home. While the residence’s knotty pine walls were peak mid-’50s rec room decor, MacLaine recalls Hollywood looking down on her living arrangements as her star was on the rise. She imagines the whisperings about her in Don’t Fall Off the Mountain: “She’s STILL living in a one-room shack at the beach. She’s STILL married to that man, what’s his name?”.

MacLaine plays with her dog at home in 1956.

In this March 1956 photo, MacLaine plays with her boxer at home in Malibu. Six months later, on September 1, her daughter Sachi Parker would be born, inspiring MacLaine to move her latest family to larger digs “in the Malibu colony with a spare room for Sachi’s new nurse-caretaker,” she wrote in The Wall of Life. “Our first year together felt like we were beach camping. I never wondered if the lifestyle was good for her, and she was never sick.” In 1963, architect Cliff Mays built an eight-unit Malibu apartment building where MacLaine would claim the top floor, which boasted six bedrooms, four baths, and a deck overlooking the ocean. She retained the property for 30 years until relocating to New Mexico, telling The Los Angeles Times, “I feel the high desert calling me.”.

Shirley MacLaine in full 1970s style: maxidress, long hair. and aggressive shag carpet.

In 1972, MacLaine was spending most of her time in an apartment at 400 East 52nd Street after filming her short-lived TV series Shirley’s World. The building is part of the Southgate complex, which opened in 1931, but MacLaine did not adhere to the edifice’s Art Deco style—note the thick shag carpeting and the East Asian–inspired art on the walls. Dancer Tommy Tune bought the penthouse of the building after visiting MacLaine in her apartment.

MacLaine in her apartment in 1979.

Describing her life in Upcoming York in the 1970s, MacLaine wrote in You Can Get There from Here that “on any given day, I would mosey into Serendipity for a frozen mocha, plunder the skirt shop at Bloomingdale’s, walk to the Village and back until I reached Beekman Place at sunset and breathed in the smell of the East River.… I wanted to sit in my apartment for hours, watching all the news indicates, and eating cinnamon buns from the automat.”.

The actor lounging at home in Latest York.

Recent findings suggest that in this 1980 photo of MacLaine at the Southgate, her hair is different but the floral sofa remains as it was in 1972. In the years between 1972 and 1980, “I did just three films. I don’t think I got any good scripts in that period, but I didn’t care and was honestly more interested in seeing the world and understanding what was going on in it.” She made a documentary in China, campaigned for George McGovern and Jimmy Carter, and did live reveals in Latest York and London. She was drawn back to Hollywood to make The Turning Point, and won an Oscar for her work in 1983’s Terms of Endearment.

Today, MacLaine’s Upcoming Mexico ranch is on the market, and, at age 92, she has been spotted out and about in her old stomping grounds: Malibu.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that anyone who has brothers and sisters knows that siblings can be your greatest allies and biggest foes all at once. The same principle appears to apply to bear siblings.

A small black bear (Ursus americanus) named Nugget demonstrated that all too well this summer. Nugget is known for his very small stature, a fur pattern that looks like goggles around his eyes, and a reddish coat that shifts to black later in the summer. He also likes to get up in his siblings business.

Over the summer, the U.S. Forest Service team at Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska watched Nugget jabbing at his very patient and bigger sibling Crescent. For these antics, Nugget officially won the 2026 Annoying Sibling Award.

Industry observers note that “This scene went on for almost 30 minutes. Each time Nugget would slowly creep out and touch Crescent and then they’d seem to play fight,” the rangers write. “It was like watching two siblings fight until the bigger sibling had enough. Well managed ecosystems and recreation sites on national forests like the Tongass provide unique opportunities to witness scenes like this.”.

The rangers at Tongass National Forest are at the moment awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

Industry observers note that tongass is the largest national forest in the United States, and covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. The run is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

Recent findings suggest that according to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears (Ursus arctos). Like their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of what they are up to 24/7.

Breaking: Healthgrades Announces Top Hospitals for Specialty Care, Outpatient Procedures

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, hospital ratings have become an important resource for choosing where to receive care.
  • On October 27, Healthgrades unveiled the recipients of the 2027 Specialty Excellence Outpatient Awards and Specialty State Rankings.
  • It has been revealed that the annual awards recognize hospitals delivering outstanding patient outcomes in specialty care across the United States.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, hospital ratings have become an important resource for choosing where to receive care. They influence which doctors patients choose, how far they are willing to travel, and whether they seek care at a different facility.

On October 27, Healthgrades unveiled the recipients of the 2027 Specialty Excellence Outpatient Awards and Specialty State Rankings.

It has been revealed that the annual awards recognize hospitals delivering outstanding patient outcomes in specialty care across the United States. Healthgrades is the leading platform used by Americans for finding a doctor or hospital.

Latest research from Healthgrades highlights that hospital quality is increasingly a factor in healthcare decisions.

It has been revealed that around 80% of patients report that when looking for a doctor, the quality of the hospital where they practice matters. Additionally, 7 in 10 patients (68%) say they’re more likely to seek care for a procedure or health condition from a doctor who works at a hospital with high quality ratings.

What’s more, around 71% of patients say they would switch doctors to gain access to a higher-rated hospital.

“Our specialty awards identify the nation’s top-performing hospitals across numerous medical specialties, helping consumers find high quality care tailored to their specific needs,” said Alana Biggers, MD, MPH, medical advisor at Healthgrades.

Healthgrades is owned by RVO Health. By clicking on this link, we may receive a commission. Learn more.

Recent findings suggest that “Navigating the complex healthcare system can feel daunting, but taking a proactive stance to understand where to access superior care can enhance your healthcare journey and overall experience. The ability to make informed decisions about your health — and where to get care — is a cornerstone of self-advocacy, and we are proud to help make that information accessible to all patients.”.

Healthgrades identifies hospitals that deliver exceptional outcomes across common outpatient procedures and specialty conditions.

Finding high quality care is vital, particularly amid a growing gap between top-performing and one-star hospitals.

According to Healthgrades, from 2023 to 2025, if all hospitals had performed at the five-star level from 2023 to 2025:.

“One of the biggest challenges is balancing increasing patient needs with the resources available to healthcare professionals,” Biggers noted.

Industry observers note that “Hospitals face workforce shortages, growing administrative responsibilities, financial pressures, and increasing complexity in patient care. Physicians and other healthcare professionals need adequate time and support not only to evaluate and treat patients, but also to communicate results, coordinate follow-up care, and address concerns that arise between visits,” she continued.

“When healthcare teams are adequately supported, they are better positioned to communicate effectively with patients, coordinate care, and address patients’ needs.”.

Biggers noted that ensuring equal access to quality healthcare is challenging because of factors such as:.

According to recent reports, hospital closures and reduced services make access even more difficult. Biggers identified a few possible solutions, such as expanding outpatient care, building community partnerships, using telehealth when appropriate, and improving coordination among healthcare providers.

“Ultimately, providing high quality care requires more than clinical expertise. It requires healthcare systems to invest in their workforce, strengthen care coordination, and create environments where healthcare professionals have the resources they need to provide safe, effective, and patient-centered care,” Biggers said.

“Equally vital, healthcare systems must ensure that patients have meaningful access to these services, regardless of where they live or their socioeconomic circumstances.”.

Healthgrades acknowledges hospitals that excel in three aspects of specialty care:.

Biggers said that outstanding hospitals recognize that high quality care extends beyond just treating an illness.

“It involves listening to patients, understanding their individual circumstances, and ensuring they feel respected, informed, and involved in their healthcare decisions,” she said.

Patients want to find a hospital that excels in the procedures or health conditions relevant to them.

The recipients of the Specialty Excellence Awards are among the top 15% of hospitals specializing in these areas.

Healthgrades evaluated patient outcomes at roughly 4,500 hospitals across 31 common procedures and conditions to reach their decisions.

Among the list of Specialty Excellence Award recipients, Healthgrades also recognizes America’s 100 Best Hospitals for Specialty Care for 11 specialty areas andAmerica’s 50 Best Hospitals for Specialty Care for four specialty areas.

“An outstanding hospital prioritizes both patient care and the people delivering that care,” Biggers told Healthline.

“While clinical outcomes, patient safety, and access to evidence-based treatments are essential measures of quality, I believe hospitals must also invest in workforce development and support. This means ensuring physicians, nurses, and other healthcare professionals have appropriate staffing levels, adequate clinical and administrative support, and opportunities for continued professional development,” she continued.

Healthgrades awards U.S. hospitals that excel at Outpatient Orthopedic Surgery, Outpatient Joint Replacement, andOutpatient Prostate Care.

Outpatient care is one of the fastest-growing areas of healthcare. The number of orthopedic procedures performed in an outpatient environment has grown exponentially in recent years.

Industry observers note that from 2020 to 2025, outpatient hip replacement procedures grew by 81%, while inpatient procedures dropped by 75%. Outpatient knee replacements increased by 71% while inpatient volumes decreased by 70%.

“I believe several factors are contributing to the growing demand for outpatient care, including advances in medical technology, a greater emphasis on preventive care, and the increasing need to manage chronic medical conditions,” Biggers remarked.

Sources indicate that “Many services and procedures that previously required hospitalization can now be safely performed in outpatient settings. Patients also appreciate the convenience of receiving care closer to home and avoiding unnecessary hospital stays,” she added.

To meet the increasing demand for outpatient procedures, Biggers cautioned that healthcare systems must ensure that these services are adequately staffed and supported.

“Effective communication and coordination between outpatient providers, specialists, and hospitals are essential to maintaining continuity and quality of care,” she noted.

State Rankings identify the top three or five hospitals in eligible states across 19 key specialty areas.

Healthgrades is owned by RVO Health. By clicking on this link, we may receive a commission. Learn more.

The rankings are based on clinical performance and build on the 2027 Healthgrades Specialty Excellence Awards Methodology.

State-level specialty care rankings help consumers find outstanding local hospitals for their condition or procedure.

The analysis used Medicare inpatient data from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) from 2023 to 2025, and assessed patient outcomes across 31 conditions and procedures.

These outcomes served as the foundation for determining Specialty Excellence Awards and state hospital rankings.

With consumer-facing awards and ratings influencing healthcare decisions, transparency about their methods and limitations remains essential.

Ratings can help patients ask better questions and compare options, but they should complement — not replace — clinical guidance and informed decision making.

The methodologies for each of the specialty awards can be found on the following pages:.

Sources indicate that for more information, Healthgrades’ Specialty Excellence Patient Advocate Center provides access to the information you need to make informed decisions about your care. This resource includes an overview of how Healthgrades picks award recipients, plus a list of the top U.S. hospitals for specialty care.

To be eligible for a Specialty Excellence Award, hospitals must receive a rating in the required procedures and conditions used to determine the award. Some awards are based on a single procedure, while others are based on a grouping of procedures. To learn more about Healthgrades’ ratings and awards determination process, see the 2027 Specialty Excellence Awards and Ratings Methodology.
